newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Explosive rally blows top off Australian dlr range.
newsitem.headline: Explosive rally blows top off Australian dlr range.

text.p: The Australian dollar was clutching gains of close to a cent late Thursday after an explosive overseas rally took the top off a range that had held since early April.

The turnaround was as unexpected as it was spectacular given the currency had spent much of the last fortnight leaning on support around US$0.7720. It owed much to the Federal Reserve's decision on Tuesday not to hike U.S. rates which squeezed many a speculator out of short dollar positions.
There was also relief key wage figures today were not the clincher for a domestic rate cut that some had billed them as.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the unit had recoiled to US$0.7830/35 from a lofty US$0.7888, but was still well up on Wednesday's late US$0.7761/66 and far above the US$0.7713 low for the week.

Dealers said a number of New York and Swiss names went on a buying spree overnight, sundering numerous resistance levels and triggering stop loss orders from those who had gone short ahead of the Fed meeting.

The break of US$0.7860 had been particularly meaningful from a technical viewpoint and left some analysts looking for an eventual assault on the US$0.7885/7905 barrier. A breach there would open the way for a return to 80 cents and beyond.
On the other hand a retreat below US$0.7780 at anytime would suggest the rally was not a true reversal of trend.

The dollar was broadly higher on the crosses at 90.50/60 yen from 88.15/25 late here Wednesday, aided by a solid bounce in US$/yen and a cooling in the feverish speculation about a Japanese rate hike. In trade weighted terms it leapt to 59.5 from just 58.6 yesterday. The U.S. currency climbed to 115.70/75 yen from 114.32/37 in New York and 113.60/70 here Wednesday.
On the domestic front a small but vocal group in the market had been touting today's final wages data as the factor which would tip the Reserve Bank's hand toward easing.
On the face of it a downward revsion in annual weekly earnings growth to 4.3 percent from 4.6 percent would seemed to have done just that.
However, the breakdown confounded expectations by showing private sector wage growth accelerated by 1.3 percent in the quarter, almost twice the pace of the 0.7 percent public rise.

The easing argument had been that aggregate wages growth was biased upwards by special circumstances in the public sector and private pay deals, which are far more important for inflation, were running at lower levels and not a danger. Some still felt that was so, but most felt the RBA would not risk it now.
"Wages growth remains too close to being a threat to the RBA's inflation target to permit another rate cut," said Stephen Roberts, an economist at UBS Australia.
"As a result, the bank will need to wait for at least another three months before it can begin to decide if wages growth is likely to moderate or accelerate," he added.
Given that the RBA expected economic growth to pick up strongly in 1997/98, by the time the wages trend was known for sure the easing argument might be academic.
Australian Finance Minister John Fahey semed to understand the RAB's dilema.
"Whether there is room as a result of this small upward movement (in wages), for a futher reduction (in rates), I think that's very much in doubt," said Fahey.
With no more wage data on the horizon, analysts were looking forward to shifting back to the real side of economy with a rash of figures out next week.

Private sector capital expenditure data for Q1 on Tuesday will be important since business investment was a cornerstone of the RBA's upbeat economic outlook. Quarterly inventories and balance of payments were also out as were monthly retail sales.
